content: 1. Ensure that the drainage channel is free from obstructions and in good condition. Remove any debris or repair the channel as necessary. Verify that gates or other access points can be securely closed and latched or locked to prevent unauthorized access. 2. Regular maintenance and repair of damaged parts or locks are essential to ensure the proper functioning of the dug well and windlass system. This includes addressing any issues identified during routine inspections. 3. Guidance on typical operations and maintenance (O&M) activities for dug wells with windlasses is provided, including recommended frequencies for each activity. These activities are critical for maintaining the functionality of the well and protecting the quality of drinking water. 4. A management advice sheet offers specific guidance for the safe management of dug wells with windlasses, supporting sanitary inspections of this drinking water source. It also outlines potential problems that may arise during inspections and provides corrective actions for each issue. 5. Sanitary inspection (SI) forms from the WHO SI packages can be used directly, but they may require adaptation to suit local contexts. Small water supplies vary widely, and some aspects of the forms may not be relevant in all settings. Additional risk factors may also need to be considered. 6. Authorities should adapt SI materials to the local context as needed, ensuring that the forms are appropriate and relevant. This adaptation can improve acceptance and uptake of the forms by users. Simplicity should remain a guiding principle during adaptation. 7. The language used in SI forms should be clear, unambiguous, and suitable for the intended users, such as surveillance officers or water suppliers. The forms should enable users to easily understand and act on identified issues. 8. Key water supply information should be captured in a user-friendly manner. This includes identifying potential sources of water contamination and communicating risk factors to water suppliers through clear, ideally graphical, representations. 9. SI forms can range from basic pictorial checklists to more detailed ones with explanatory notes and guidance. Mobile applications or other digital tools may also be used to support inspections and data collection. 10. Inspectors should be provided with technical guidance on the key features of the water supply system as they relate to the SI form questions. This includes identifying appropriate corrective actions for issues found during inspections. 11. Basic information should be provided to inform key operations and maintenance activities that protect water quality and ensure reliable functioning of the water supply system. 12. Adaptation of SI packages should consider factors such as language translation, local risk factors, and cultural or religious practices. Questions that are irrelevant should be removed, and additional questions should be included where necessary. 13. Risk factors in SI forms may require differential weighting based on local conditions. For example, an unlocked gate may pose less risk than a latrine located uphill from a water source in sandy soil. Local conditions should guide the prioritization of actions. 14. Minimum safe distances (MSDs) between water sources and potential contamination sources should be determined based on local hydrological characteristics. This includes considering soil permeability, pathogen travel time, and other site-specific factors. 15. MSDs may vary significantly depending on the permeability of the soil or rock. For example, impermeable clays may require only a few meters, while permeable gravel beds may necessitate several kilometers of separation. 16. In the absence of detailed hydrogeological information, test drilling and infiltration tests around the water source can provide insights into local conditions. This includes assessing soil infiltration capacity and identifying fissures or joints that may increase hydraulic conductivity. 17. Field testing of adapted SI packages should be conducted to ensure they are fit for purpose. This may involve piloting in select areas, comparing inspection site photos with completed reports, and interviewing users of the SI packages. 18. Feedback from field testing should inform further revisions and improvements to the SI packages. Updates should be made over time as additional experience is gained and lessons are learned. 19. Technical guidance and management advice should be tailored to the local technology and resources available. Operations, maintenance, and troubleshooting advice should be pragmatic and aligned with local capacity. 20. Hydrogeological information, where available, should be used to inform risk assessments and determine appropriate MSDs. In the absence of such data, conservative estimates should be used to ensure safety. 21. Relocation of water sources or sanitation infrastructure, or the use of alternative sanitation designs (e.g., elevated pits or sealed pits with impermeable linings), may be necessary to mitigate contamination risks. 22. For more information on conducting risk assessments for groundwater contamination, refer to guidelines such as Guidelines for assessing the risk to groundwater from on-site sanitation and Protecting groundwater for health.
